segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I think it's probably about two litres.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Ah, well, the number many people have heard is two litres a day.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Of course, everyone needs to drink some water.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Over half the human body is made up of it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But exactly how much water do we need to stay healthy?

segments.speaker: Beth

segments.text: Great. But first, I have a question for you, Phil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I mentioned that over half the human body consists of water, but there's an even higher percentage of water in our blood.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But how much Is our blood A around 80 water B around 90 water or C 100 water

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I think it around 80 water

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK I will reveal the correct answer later in the programme

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Our blood needs water so it can carry nutrients to the body's cells and organs.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The amount recommended is often given as two litres a day.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But why?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here to discuss this with BBC World Service programme,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The Food Chain, is biologist, Professor John Speakman.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So I'm not sure how it was arrived at, but it seems to be a number that has taken grip on a very large number of countries.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So if you look at government recommendations around the world, they're pretty much all the same.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: They pretty much all say everybody's got to be drinking two litres of water.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Professor Speakman doesn't know how the number of two litres a day was arrived at, how it was decided or calculated.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Nevertheless, the idea of drinking two litres a day has taken grip on many governments around the world.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: When you say an idea has taken grip on something, you mean it's taken control of it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yes, Professor Speakman says that pretty much all governments are giving pretty much the same recommendation.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: He uses the phrase pretty much to mean almost.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: For example, pretty much all governments advise drinking two litres a day means almost all governments advise it.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: What Professor Speakman doesn't have, however, is any scientific evidence for this advice.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The number of exactly two litres isn based on scientific fact It more of a ballpark figure a number which is a guess but which you still believe is approximately correct

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Actually, the amount of water in our bodies is changing all the time. Like your bank balance,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: which goes down when you spend money. Your body loses water all the time when you breathe,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: sweat or go to the toilet. Exactly how much you need to drink depends on how much water your body

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: needs to replace and that mainly depends on your size.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But what happens when we drink less than we

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: should? Here's hydration expert Dr Nidia Rodriguez-Sanchez describing the effects of dehydration

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: to BBC World Service's The Food Chain. And also many times we start getting dehydrated and we

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: don't realise we are dehydrated so it's very common that we feel tired or we feel like with a bit of a

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: headache or even we think we are hungry. We go and get some food and actually what is happening

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: is that we are thirsty, that we are dehydrated. We're starting to show some signs or some symptoms

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: of dehydration. Dr Sanchez describes the effect of dehydration, the condition of not having enough

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: water in your body so that you feel ill or weak. She mentions feeling tired, having a headache or

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: a dry mouth as symptoms of dehydration. Symptoms are signs or feelings in the body showing the

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: presence of some illness or condition

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So whether you drink a little more or a little less it seems that around two litres of water a day is a good way to keep your blood and body healthy Speaking of which Phil it time to reveal the answer to my

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: question. What percentage of our blood is water? You said 80% and the answer is 90%. Our blood

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: consists of around 90% water. Okay, let's recap the vocabulary we've used, starting with the phrase

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to arrive at a number, meaning to decide it by doing calculations.

segments.text: If an idea takes grip on

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: something, it takes control of it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The phrase pretty much means almost. For example, pretty much

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: everyone likes chocolate, which means almost everyone likes chocolate.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: A ballpark figure

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: is a phrase meaning a number which is an acceptably accurate approximation.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Dehydration is the condition of not having enough water in your body

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: so that you feel ill or weak.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And finally, a symptom is a sign or feeling in the body

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: showing the presence of an illness or condition.
